H01:
*If this is your first time at this section,* the clock over the Atrium's own information desk already shows a time you don't remember reaching. The escalators stand stopped halfway to galleries that go nowhere, and nothing hums. Three ways lead out, each lit its own colour: the Concourse in cold blue, Duty-Free under a gold arch that smells of frying oil, and the skybridge to the hotel, where a few windows are lit and nothing moves. Beneath the escalators, a strip light burns over a hatch marked LOST & FOUND. Sam glances back once at his cities. "Glasshaven's on time," he says. "Nothing was ever late in Glasshaven. I wouldn't allow it."

*If you have been here before,* the clock over the desk has jumped again while your back was turned, and one more escalator climbs to nothing.

*If you hold one or none of the BOARDING PASS, the PASSPORT and the LAST PAGE,* the tall passenger is at the far end, past the stopped escalators, its coat pooled on the marble. It holds its sign a little higher than before, in case you missed it.

*If you hold two of them,* it waits halfway across the floor, among the planters. It stands with its back to you. Its sign is turned round to face you.

*If you hold all three,* it is standing at the foot of the newest escalator, close enough that you can hear the cardboard of its sign creak in its grip. Across the floor, the corridor to Gate 0 is lit white.

If you take the Concourse towards the gates, turn to {C01}.

If you have not yet found the LAST PAGE, and you go under the gold arch to Duty-Free and the Food Court, turn to {F01}.

If you do not yet have the PASSPORT, and you cross the skybridge to the Airport Hotel, turn to {O01}.

If you haven't already been to the Lost & Found hatch beneath the escalators, its strip light is on. To go there, turn to {H04}.

If you hold the BOARDING PASS, the PASSPORT and the LAST PAGE, the corridor to Gate 0 is lit for you. Turn to {G43}.
H05:
You come back into the Atrium, and the board answers before you are halfway across the floor.

Every row turns over, a long rolling clatter, and the cities go past too fast to read. When it stops, the final boarding time hasn't changed. The clock beneath it has. 05:59 is closer than it was a minute ago. You have lost time you never spent.

Beside the board, a screen you hadn't noticed has come on. *FLIGHT TRACKER*, it says in the corner, though there are no planes on it. It's the terminal seen from above: grey corridors on black, the Atrium a pale circle in the middle, and in the circle, one green dot where you are standing.

A red dot sits in the corridor just behind the circle. It doesn't blink. When you take a step back, it slides forward into the next room and stops. It doesn't gain. It doesn't fall behind.

*If Sam is with you,* a second green dot blinks beside yours. Sam steps left and his dot goes with him. "So we keep moving," he says, in a practical voice you've never heard him use.

*If you have the codeword LOST,* a second green dot blinks fast at the far edge of the map, in a room with no walls drawn round it.

The red dot is always one room behind you. Note the codeword RETURNED.

If Sam is with you, turn to {H11}.

Otherwise, turn to {H01}.
H11:
Sam drops onto the end of a row of seats under the board, and you sit down one seat along from him. He has his phone out, and the screen lights his face from underneath. Three per cent.

He isn't looking for signal. He's scrolling, up and up, through three years, until he stops and holds the phone out. He doesn't give it to you. He makes you look.

It's the thread. Yours and his. Your messages are long and grey: questions, a photo of a lake, *how did the scan go*, *should I come for his birthday*. His are blue, and all the same.

*We're fine.*

*We're fine.*

*We're fine x*

You remember the x. Two Christmases ago. You read it on a tram and missed your stop.

"I had it saved," Sam says. "W, and the phone did the rest."

"You had a lot on. I got it."

"I didn't have a lot on." He says it to the board. "I wanted you where you were. He'd hear the front door and look up, and it'd be me, and he'd be glad anyway. I liked that. I liked being the one he got."

"Sam—"

"Do you remember what I said? At the airport?"

You do. He drove. Radio up so neither of you had to talk. At the departures gate, where the people who aren't flying have to stop, he didn't hug you. He said, *Go on, then. Don't bother coming back.*

"And you didn't," he says. "I said it once. You took it like a ticket."

"You told me you were fine. For three years."

"You're thirty-four. You can read between two words."

The screen dims. One per cent. The last blue bubble sits there: *We're fine.* It goes black, and his face goes dark with it.

If you tell him you should have come anyway, turn to {H12}.

If you have the codeword CARE, you can say nothing at all, and put your own phone in his hand, the thread open from your side. To do that, turn to {H12}.

If you tell him he never asked you to, turn to {H13}.
H12:
*If you told him you should have come anyway,* it comes out too quiet, so you say it again. "Whatever you sent. I knew what *fine* meant. I've always known what you mean by *fine*." Sam turns the phone over and puts it face down on his knee. You know that move. It's yours.

*If you gave him your own phone instead,* he reads it. Your side of the thread: every long grey message, every question he answered with two words. He scrolls up a long way before he stops. He doesn't give it back. He holds it in his lap, screen down, both hands over it.

*If you have TOLD,* you don't need to say the rest of it, the gate in March and the pass you never used. You've said it once tonight. He knows.

For a while there's only the board, turning over and finding nothing new.

"You should have come," he says at last. "And I should have stopped typing it."

Nobody says sorry. Nobody gets up.

He says, "He kept your postcards. On the fridge, picture side out, so people would ask. 'That's where Kite is,' he'd tell them, tapping whichever was newest." Note the codeword TRUCE.

Turn to {H01}.
H13:
"You never asked me to."

It comes out harder than you meant. Three years of blue bubbles are in it.

Sam looks at the black screen for a long time.

"No," he says. "I didn't."

*If you have TOLD,* he adds, "I said that already. At the sunglasses." It costs him more the second time.

The rest of it should come now. The *but*. It doesn't.

"Go on, then," he says, and stops dead. You both hear it: the first half of the line, in the same voice, three years older. One corner of his mouth pulls tight. He shakes his head once, short, the way you'd shake off water.

"I said that," he says. "At the gate. I meant it when I said it. I meant it for about a year." He looks at the floor. "Then I didn't know how to stop meaning it. So I kept typing the other thing."

He doesn't say sorry. You notice, and he sees you notice, and neither of you moves to fill the gap.

He gets up. He doesn't walk off. He stands at the end of the row with the phone in his fist, and when you get up too, he waits until you're level before he goes.

Turn to {H01}.
H03:
You are halfway across the Atrium floor when the chime comes.

*Ding-dong.*

Softly, this time, from the speaker directly above you and nowhere else.

*If Sam is with you,* he has stopped under the board with his back to you, and he doesn't turn round.

A voice comes. It isn't the Announcer's smooth, unhurried calm.

*If you do not have FORGOT,* it's lower, rough at the edges: a voice that gave up smoking twice and hummed along to the news. Your father's voice, with the little catch in it before he said anything he meant.

*If you have FORGOT,* you don't know the voice; the sound of him is gone. You know it only because it says *There you are*, the way the words always went, and because Sam has gone white.

*There you are. It's all right, love. You've done enough.*

*If you have the codeword LOST,* it goes on, gently: *Sam's already boarded. He's saved you a seat. You may join him now.*

Otherwise, it goes on: *Leave Sam with us, and you may board now.*

It says your name. All of it: first, middle, last, each one set down separately, as if it's copying them off a form.

He never did that. Not once in thirty-four years. Not when you dented the car. Not when you rang to say you'd taken the job abroad. Not on the last birthday card, in capitals gone shaky: *LOVE YOU KITE.*

He called you Kite because you always flew off, and he called you that to the end. Kite, every time. Whatever is speaking knows his voice and his words. It doesn't know that.

The voice waits. Down the corridor towards Gate 0, a light comes on over an empty seat, and you know without looking that it's by a window. Note the codeword HEARD.

If you accept, and walk towards Gate 0 without him, turn to {AL01}.

If you refuse, turn to {H06}.
H06:
You don't look up at the ceiling. You turn your back on the speaker and give it the only answer it's getting, to the room and not to it: "No."

*If Sam is with you,* he has sat back down on the end of the row under the board, saying the cities half aloud: Glasshaven, Port Ever, Saint Undermere. "What did it want?" he asks. "Nothing," you say. "We'll wait. Together." He goes on with the cities. *If you also have TRUCE,* he gets as far as Saint Undermere, then lifts his bag off the seat beside him.

Above you, the speaker gives a small wet click, like a tongue leaving teeth. When the voice comes back, it has stopped trying to be anyone at all.

*Then we'll wait together,* it says.

All around the Atrium, faintly, seats creak: the sound of a great many people settling in for a long delay. Gain 1 Fear.

Turn to {H01}.
AL01:
You walk.

It's simple. One foot, then the other, across the marble towards the corridor where Gate 0 glows. The floor is clean and the light is kind, and with every step the weight you've carried for three years gets lighter. You're setting it down behind you, piece by piece, for someone else to pick up. Someone else always has.

*If Sam is with you,* his voice comes from under the board. "Kite." He isn't shouting. He says it the way Dad said it, and you'd forgotten he had the right to. *If you have FORGOT,* you can't hear that; you only know the word was Dad's. "Kite. Where are you going?" A pause, and lower: "Kite, please."

*If you have the codeword LOST,* his voice comes from every speaker in the Atrium, small and far off: "Kite. Kite, please."

You stop.

Ahead, the corridor is bright and quiet. A window seat is waiting. Nobody there will need anything from you again.

If you turn back, turn to {H01}.

If you keep walking, turn to {E_ALONE}.
H04:
The Lost & Found is a hatch in the wall beneath the escalators: a brass bell on the counter, a strip light humming to itself. You ring. Nobody comes. The shutter is up.

Behind the counter, shelves run back further than the wall should allow, into a dimness that smells of damp cardboard and old rain. A personal stereo with orange foam headphones. One small red shoe. Umbrellas from every decade. A tray of reading glasses folded up like sleeping moths. A teddy bear with a luggage label round its neck: *1998*.

A handwritten card is taped to the counter.

*ONE ITEM PER PASSENGER.*

Three things have been set out apart from the rest. A heavy black torch, the old steel kind. A green first-aid kit with a faded white cross. A brown leather luggage tag on a buckled strap.

You turn the tag over. Your name is on it, in handwriting you don't recognise.

You can only take something you don't already have written on your Adventure Sheet. Whatever you take, you have a feeling this hatch won't open for you twice.

If you take the torch, turn to {H07}.

If you take the first-aid kit, turn to {H08}.

If you do not have the codeword TRANSFER, and you take the luggage tag with your name on it, turn to {H09}.
H07:
The torch is heavier than it looks, a steel tube wrapped in black tape where the grip has worn through. Someone has scratched a tally into the barrel, dozens of short lines. You click it on.

The beam comes out yellow and wide, and where it lands, the Atrium changes.

The plastic ferns in the nearest planter are brown and dead and real. A smear on the marble you'd taken for a shadow is a long scuff of fingermarks, dragged towards the Gate 0 corridor.

On the pillar, an old Larkvale poster shows a departure lounge full of smiling holidaymakers. Under the beam, every one of them has turned to look at the same empty seat at the front.

You switch it off. The ferns are green. The holidaymakers smile at the camera.

Dad kept the bathroom scales turned to the wall for thirty years and called it peace of mind.

Note the TORCH on your Adventure Sheet.

Behind you, the Lost & Found shutter rattles down by itself, all the way to the counter, and the light behind it goes out.

Turn to {H01}.
H08:
The first-aid kit is a green plastic box, the white cross faded to the colour of milky tea, the clasp stiff. Inside: bandages in paper wrappers, safety pins, a foil blanket folded to the size of a wallet, a small brown bottle that smells of your grandmother's bathroom cabinet.

Every item is dated in biro on a strip of tape. *1998.*

It's the most ordinary thing you've touched tonight. You hold it a moment longer than you need to.

*If Sam is with you,* he takes it off you without asking. He goes through it the way a nurse would: unrolls a bandage an inch, sniffs the bottle, checks the pins. "Tape's perished. Rest is fine." He snaps it shut and gives it back. He doesn't say where he learned.

Note the FIRST-AID KIT on your Adventure Sheet. Once, at any time, you may open it to restore 6 Vigour (never above its starting score), then cross it off.

Behind you, the Lost & Found shutter rattles down by itself, and the light goes out.

Turn to {H01}.
H09:
The tag is soft with handling, the leather dark at the edges from being held. On the front, in red capitals, the old printed way:

*TRANSFER*

On the back, in the same writing as your name, small, pressed so hard the pen nearly went through:

*Connections are made by number, not by gate. Seat 1A has been held since 1998.*

You read it twice. Held. For whom? A seat kept empty all that time. You picture a whole lounge of people sitting round it, looking at it, until whoever it's held for comes to sit down.

*If Sam is with you,* he takes it off you. "That's a threat," he says. "That's a threat written by someone who's been on a customer service course." He turns the tag over twice himself. "Number of what, though?" He gives it back.

Note the codeword TRANSFER. Behind you, the Lost & Found shutter rattles down by itself, and the light goes out.

Turn to {H01}.
C01:
*If you have been here before,* the numbers are wrong again. Go straight to the choices below.

The Concourse runs away from the Atrium in a long bright tube of carpet and glass, gates opening off it on either side.

The gate numbers hang from the ceiling on lit blue signs. You read them as you walk, and they won't add up. 23. 6. 41. 6.

You stop under the second 6 and look back at the first. Same scuff in the corner of the sign. Same row of empty seats, same paper coffee cup on the same armrest.

*If Sam is with you,* he goes to look at the cup and comes back shaking out his wrist. "Warm," he says, as if it bit him.

Ahead, the Concourse splits. To the left, the low-numbered gates, where a crowd seems to be breathing. Straight on, a sheet of paper is taped to a pillar, with an arrow drawn in marker and two words: *Gates 00*.

If you head towards the low-numbered gates, turn to {C02}.

If you follow the paper sign for Gates 00, turn to {C10}.
C02:
*If you have been here before,* the rows are just as you left them. Go straight to the choices below.

The low gates are full.

Every seat in every bolted row has someone in it, sitting the way people sit at three in the morning when they've given up on sleep: coats on, bags on laps, chins tipped forward. None of them moves. You can't hear any of them breathe, and yet the gate is full of slow breathing.

Their clothes are wrong. Shoulder pads. Shell suits. A mobile phone the size of a shoe on a man's belt. A boy in a football shirt with a sponsor you remember from the playground.

Their skin is the grey of old newspaper. Some have sat so long the seats have begun to grow up round them, plastic softening over hips and wrists. The Delayed.

*If Sam is with you,* he takes the far side of the aisle, bag hugged to his chest, giving every grey knee the small apologetic duck he gives people in cinemas. *If you also have TRUCE,* he nods at a purple shell suit and mouths, *Yours?* For a second he's the old Sam, who ran commentary on your clothes. You'd missed him.

Near the front, an old man in a brown cardigan turns his head. You hear his neck as it goes. His gaze finds you and stays, the only one in the room that moves.

He lifts his wrist a little off the armrest, and holds it there, for you.

If you have not already made him a promise, and you go and talk to the old man, turn to {C03}.

If you keep your head down and slip past the rows towards the gate desk beyond, turn to {C06}.
C03:
Up close he smells of airline blankets and peppermints. A paper boarding pass pokes out of his cardigan pocket, soft as cloth from handling.

*If you have been here before,* he doesn't say you're new. He says, "You came back," and looks at your wrist. Go straight to the choices.

"You're new," he says. His voice is thin and kind. "Don't sit down, whatever you do. They'll tell you it won't be long." He smiles. "Walter."

He doesn't offer to shake. His right arm has gone into the armrest up to the wrist.

"LV 137," he says, before you can ask. "Nineteen ninety-eight. Little hop home for my girl's birthday. We never boarded. Sat here with the plane right there through the glass, all night, and the captain kept saying a short delay. *A short delay, folks, thank you for your patience.* By three in the morning people stopped asking."

He looks along the rows, all those bowed grey heads.

"By four, they started…" He stops. "…joining up."

"Joining up how?"

Walter doesn't answer. He looks to the far end of the Concourse, back towards the Atrium, and keeps looking long enough that you look too. The far end is empty. When you turn back, he's talking about his daughter.

"My Ruth was meeting me at arrivals. She'd have waited. Stood there with a sign, knowing her." His eyes fill. "If you get out of here, tell her I tried."

If you promise him, turn to {C04}.

If you tell him you can't promise anything, turn to {C05}.
C04:
"I promise," you say. You don't ask yourself whether it's true.

Walter digs in his cardigan pocket, brings out the boarding pass and presses it on you, folding your fist round it with his own. His skin is cool and dry. "No use to me now," he says. "Go on. Look."

You look. The name printed across the top in old dot-matrix capitals is yours. *LV 137.* The rest has faded to nothing.

"There," Walter says. "That's done, then."

He settles back into the chair and lets it have him. The grey plastic comes up softly over his other wrist, over his elbow, and he sighs the way Dad sighed dropping into his armchair after a long drive. His eyes stay on you until they close.

Ruth. You say it under your breath so you won't lose it. Ruth, at arrivals, with a sign.

*If Sam is with you,* he isn't looking at Walter. He's looking at you, and he keeps looking until you look back.

Gain 1 Fear. Note the BOARDING PASS on your Adventure Sheet, and note the codeword PROMISE.

Along the rows, the Delayed settle a little lower. Turn to {C09}.
C05:
"I can't," you say. "I can't promise anything. I don't even know the way out."

Walter nods slowly, as if it's the answer he's had from everyone. His left arm comes off the armrest, and his grip closes round your wrist.

It isn't an old man's grip. It's a dozen grips at once. There are more fingers on your wrist than one hand has. "Please," he says, and there are other voices under his, all of them saying please. Along the rows, heads begin to lift.

It takes everything you have to prise his grip open, one joint at a time. The last lets go with the crack of a green stick.

*If Sam is with you,* half the prising is his, and he swears the whole while. "Sorry," he says to Walter, absurdly. "Sorry. Sorry." The moment you're clear he lets go of you and steps back. *If you also have TRUCE,* he keeps hold of your sleeve instead, until you're past the last seat.

Your wrist is a bracelet of bruises. Lose 2 Vigour.

Behind you, the heads go down again, one by one. Ahead, past the last seat, a desk light is on. Turn to {C06}.
C06:
*If you have been here before,* she is typing again, as if you never came. Go straight to the choices below.

Past the last of the seats, the carpet changes, blue giving way to an older red and navy, and you've stepped over a line into another decade.

There's a gate desk here, lit. A woman in a Larkvale uniform sits behind it: navy jacket, red piping, hair in a tight bun. She is typing. On her screen, green on black, the same line runs down the page, again and again, the same length every time. She finishes it, presses return, and starts again.

Tucked into the cuff of her sleeve, the corner of a boarding pass sticks out, the old card kind, soft and grey with handling.

Above her, a television is bolted high on the wall, the boxy kind with a curved glass screen. It's showing the news with the sound off. Every few seconds the picture rolls.

Behind the desk, a dot-matrix printer chatters to itself, feeding out a long ribbon of paper with holes punched down both edges.

On the next pillar along, another sheet of paper with the same marker arrow. *Gates 00.*

*If Sam is with you,* he says, without moving his lips, "She knows we're here."

The typing doesn't stop. It doesn't need to.

If you do not have a BOARDING PASS, and you approach the desk, turn to {C07}.

If you stand under the television and watch the news, turn to {C19}.

If you do not have the codeword INCIDENT, and you want to read what the printer is printing, turn to {C37}.

If you keep walking, turn to {C10}.
C37:
You edge round the end of the desk. The woman doesn't look up. The printer head shuttles back and forth, hammering out each line in tiny dots, and the paper smells hot.

*LARKVALE AIRWAYS. IRREGULAR OPERATIONS REPORT.*

*FLT LV 137. GATE 0. 23 NOV 98. STATUS: NOT DEPARTED.*

*CREW ON DUTY:*

The head types a name. It goes back over it and types X after X until the name is a black bar. It does it again. And again. Five names, five bars.

One name it leaves alone.

*MARGARET (PURSER).*

*0310. PASSENGERS INCREASINGLY DISTRESSED. ONE (1) PASSENGER OBSERVED AT GATE, NOT ON PASSENGER LIST.*

*0340. CREW MEMBER READ THE PASSENGER LIST ALOUD. SUBJECT REMAINED STATIONARY FOR THE DURATION.*

*0412. LIST COMPLETED. SUBJECT*

The line stops. The head hangs over the gap, humming, then jumps to the next line.

The printer feeds out one blank sheet, then another, then stops. Nothing else is coming. You tear the report off along the perforations and fold it small.

*If Sam is with you,* he taps the name. "Margaret," he says. "Hi, Margaret."

Note the codeword INCIDENT. The typing has stopped. When you look up, the woman at the desk is watching the printer, not you. You leave before she starts again, following the paper arrows. Turn to {C10}.
C19:
You step under the television until you can read the strip along the bottom.

*BREAKING: LARKVALE FLIGHT MYSTERY*

The picture rolls, steadies. Dawn footage, blue and grainy, shot through a wire fence: an aircraft at a gate with the jet bridge attached and every window dark. You know the shape of the terminal behind it. You're standing in it.

Captions crawl beneath the newsreader in blocky white letters, a beat behind her mouth.

*FLIGHT LV 137, DUE TO DEPART ON THE NIGHT OF 23/11/1998, WAS FOUND AT ITS GATE THIS MORNING, DOORS CLOSED. THE AIRCRAFT NEVER LEFT THE GATE. NONE OF ITS 137 PASSENGERS HAVE BEEN LOCATED.*

The date in the corner of the screen says 1998.

The newsreader finishes her sentence. And she stops reading. Her head turns away from the camera she should be looking into, a fraction at a time, and she looks straight out of the screen and down. At you. The captions crawl on without her.

She doesn't blink. Neither do you, until your eyes sting.

The picture rolls. When it settles, she's reading again. Gain 1 Fear.

You walk on, fast, after the paper arrows, and you don't look back at the screen. Turn to {C10}.
C07:
You walk up to the desk. The typing doesn't stop.

Up close you can read the screen. It's one line, typed again and again down the page: your surname, a comma, the letter *R*. *SEAT 1A.* At the end of every line the system has added two words of its own: *NO SHOW.*

She types it again. Return. Again.

"Good evening," she says, still typing. Her voice is beautifully trained. "Thank you for flying Larkvale. Boarding pass, please."

You don't have one. You have a phone with no signal and a pocketful of receipts from another airport.

She reaches out with her left. Her right goes on typing. The old boarding pass has slid a little further out of her cuff, and you can read part of it now: *STAFF STANDBY. 23 NOV 98. 23:55.* The last flight out that night. Once LV 137 was away, she'd have been on her way home too.

"Boarding pass, please," she says again, in the same voice, with the same small smile.

The printer beside her keyboard gives a short whirr, warming up.

*If Sam is with you,* he murmurs in your ear: "Say you checked in online. Everyone checks in online."

If you bluff, turn to {C08}.

If you back away and keep walking, turn to {C10}.
C08:
You pat your pockets with a small performance of irritation, the way people do at real desks. "Sorry. I checked in online. It's on my phone, but there's no signal, and the man at the other desk said you could reprint it for me here."

It comes out smooth. You've lied in airports before. You've lied to Dad from airports, on bad lines, in this exact voice: *I'll try to get back next month.*

For the first time, her typing stops. She waits at the keys. The cursor blinks at the end of your father's surname, which is also yours.

She looks at you and waits, and you can't tell whether she wants you to be telling the truth.

Test your Nerve. If you succeed, turn to {C32}. If you fail, turn to {C30}.
C32:
She looks at you a moment longer. She goes back to the keys.

"Of course," she says. "I'll reprint that for you now. Name?"

There it is. The question this airport keeps asking. You hear the Handbook in your head: *Never give your name.* You give it anyway, because the printer is already running, because you need this, because she asked so nicely.

She types it slowly, one key at a time, and you watch it go in.

The printer chatters and pushes out a pass. She tears it off along the perforations and slides it across the desk.

*LV 137. GATE 0. SEAT 1A.*

The same seat as the line on her screen, the one marked NO SHOW. She has put you in it.

"Enjoy your flight," she says, and her smile widens a little too far, the corners still travelling after the rest of her face has stopped.

She turns back to the screen. Return. She starts typing again, and the line isn't your father's any more. It's yours. Return. Yours. Return.

Note the BOARDING PASS on your Adventure Sheet. Add 1 to your Claim.

Turn to {C09}.
C30:
She doesn't stop smiling. "I'm afraid I can't help you without a valid boarding pass," she says, and stands.

She stands, and keeps standing. Her chair rolls back. Her shoulders rise past where shoulders stop, the navy jacket stretching, its seams straining, her neck lengthening with a soft creak of gristle, until she's looking down at you from somewhere near the television. The boarding pass in her cuff doesn't move.

"Please," she says, and her arm comes down over the desk towards your face, gently, the way you'd reach to straighten someone's collar.

*If Sam is with you,* he grabs the stapler off the desk and stands at your shoulder, white to the lips.

GROUND STAFF   NERVE 8   VIGOUR 8

If you win, turn to {C31}.

If your Vigour reaches 0, turn to {D_VIGOUR}.
C31:
She folds. There isn't another word for it. Her long body hinges at too many places and settles back behind the desk, and then she's sitting again, small and ordinary.

The boarding pass has slipped out of her cuff onto the keyboard. *STAFF STANDBY. 23 NOV 98.* She looks at it for a long moment. She tucks it back into her sleeve, corner first, with great care.

"Thank you," she says, and you don't know what for.

The printer hasn't stopped. A pass is jammed halfway out of the slot, the machine whining as it tries to push out the rest. You grab it and pull. It tears with a long ragged sound and leaves you the top two-thirds: *LV 137. GATE 0.* Below that, a smear where the seat should be.

Your name is already printed across the top. She never asked for it.

*If Sam is with you,* he puts the stapler down on the desk, squared to the edge, as if he's tidying up after a visit. He's shaking. So are you.

Note the BOARDING PASS on your Adventure Sheet.

Turn to {C09}.
C09:
The pass sits in your inside pocket, stiff against your ribs.

You keep reaching in to touch it, checking it's there. It's a ticket for LV 137, and you think of an aircraft that never left its gate, and you stop reaching.

*If Sam is with you,* he glances at the pass. "Framed," he says. That's all. He's already walking, and you have to supply the rest yourself: the downstairs toilet, the wall of old boarding passes over the cistern. *If you also have TRUCE,* a few steps on, he supplies it himself: "Downstairs toilet, with the others." For a second you're both laughing in a dead airport.

Ahead, the Concourse runs back towards the Atrium. The gate signs have stopped changing their minds. Behind you, they are starting to go out.

Turn to {C35}.
C35:
Halfway back to the Atrium, the gate you've just left goes dark behind you.

*Clunk.* The heavy sound of a breaker being thrown. Then the gate before it. *Clunk.* The dark comes up the Concourse at walking pace, one gate behind you, never two.

You don't hear footsteps. You hear breathing. It's in the gate you walked out of a minute ago: slow and wet, too many lungs for one throat.

It doesn't come out. It stays in the room behind you, and when you move on, so does the room. Gain 1 Fear.

*If Sam is with you,* he has stopped walking. "Don't run," he says. "It doesn't run." His voice is steady, and it nearly works on you.

The Atrium is three hundred metres ahead. You could walk it backwards, facing the dark doorway the whole way, so it can't move while you're looking. Every second you watch, it watches back.

Or you could walk blind, with that sound at your back the whole way.

Tick one hour on your Adventure Sheet.

If you have just ticked your sixth hour, turn to {E_FINALCALL}.

If you turn and watch the doorway until you reach the Atrium, add 1 to your Claim: it learns your face. If you shut your eyes and walk, holding on to Sam if you can, gain 1 more Fear.

Either way, when you reach the Atrium: if you do not have the codeword RETURNED, turn to {H05}. If you have RETURNED but not HEARD, turn to {H03}. If you have both, turn to {H01}.
C10:
*If you have been here before,* he is still out there, waving, a little nearer the glass. *If Sam is with you,* he won't look. Go straight to the choices.

The paper arrows lead you on and down, past gates with no numbers at all, to where the Concourse stops pretending.

A sign hangs over an empty gate, lit the same blue as all the others: *00*.

The windows here show no night. Where the apron should be there is only white, flat and total and shadowless, a page with nothing on it. You can't see the ground. You can't see the sky.

Out in it, a man in a long grey wool coat is waving.

He's fifty metres out, standing on nothing, one arm swinging slowly from side to side. Dad never waved like that. He gave you one quick salute from the viewing deck and turned back to the planes. This one doesn't stop. Even from here you can see he is smiling, and the arm goes on, side to side, long after anyone would have seen him.

Beside the windows is the jet bridge door: grey steel, a push bar, a small wired window full of white.

*If you have the codeword LOST,* it looks like a door again. You know better.

*If Sam is with you,* he has gone right up to it. He reaches for the bar, shaking, and doesn't touch it. You watch him decide not to, over and over. "Don't," he says, though you haven't moved. "The book said. Double zero. It said—" He can't finish.

If you go to the window to see him properly, knowing it will see you properly too, turn to {C11}.

If Sam is with you, you can turn your back on the window and pull him away. Turn to {C12}.

If you open the jet bridge door at Gate 00, turn to {D03}.

If you turn your back on the window and walk away up the Concourse, turn to {C18}.
D03:
You push the bar. The door opens, as if it's been waiting for someone with the nerve.

Behind you, a voice shouts. It might be Sam's. The door closes on it with a soft hydraulic sigh.

The jet bridge is carpeted and slopes gently down. The little windows along its walls are full of white. You walk towards the aircraft door at the far end, and it doesn't get closer. You walk faster. Ten minutes. An hour. When you look back, the door you came through is a pinprick.

You keep walking. After a while your feet stop hurting. Your watch stops at 05:59 and stays there, and you stop checking it.

Gate 00 does not exist. The Handbook said so. You remember that, for a while, and then you don't.

Somewhere ahead, faintly, a warm voice is apologising for the short delay. You are still walking.

Add 1 to your Claim. Return to {C01} and choose again.
C11:
You go to the window.

The glass is so cold it burns. Frost blooms out from where you touch it, white ferns of ice spreading across the pane, and on the other side, much closer than he was, stands your father.

It's him. Almost. The grey coat with the one button that never matched. The aftershave, which you can smell through the glass, which is impossible. His hair as it was before the treatment, before he got thin. He's smiling with his whole face, the smile he kept for arrivals.

He lifts a hand and lays it flat on the glass, opposite yours.

He says your name. Not Kite. Your name, and the glass carries it to you muffled, from under water. Somewhere low in your chest, you answer to it.

His other arm is waving. Down by his side, slowly, the same steady swing. He's here. It hasn't stopped.

*If Sam is with you,* he's crying beside you. Not loudly. He stands with his arms at his sides and his face coming apart. "He looks well," he says. "He looks so well."

Gain 2 Fear. Add 1 to your Claim.

If Sam is with you and you have the codeword TRUCE or THAW, turn to {C13}.

If Sam is with you and you have neither, turn to {C14}.

If you have the codeword LOST, stay at the glass until the frost closes over his face, then walk back up the Concourse without turning round. Turn to {C18}.
C12:
You take Sam by the arm. "Come on. We're going."

He doesn't move. He's staring past you at the white, at the waving man. "Hang on."

"It's not him."

"I know it's not him." He wrenches his arm free so hard his elbow bangs the glass. "I'm not stupid. I was there, remember? I was holding his hand when he—" He stops. Swallows.

"I want one minute with it," he says. Quiet now. "One minute."

The right thing to say is in your mouth somewhere. You walk anyway.

Behind you, the glass gives one soft knock, the knuckle of someone who expects to be let in. You don't look. At the edge of sight the grey sleeve goes on swinging, in no hurry at all.

His footsteps come at last, and stay well back.

*If you have TRUCE,* they catch you up before the next gate. "You owe me that minute," Sam says. "Don't think I won't collect."

Gates 00 falls away behind you. The numbers overhead go by in an order that almost makes sense, then doesn't: 12, 19, 12. Ahead, the corridor opens out into a round hall.

Turn to {C18}.
C13:
You don't know how long you stand there. Long enough for the frost to spread to the size of a dinner plate. Long enough for the man in the coat to lower his arm at last and simply watch.

Sam turns from the window first. He steps sideways and leans into you, shoulder against shoulder, then his forehead against the side of your head, the whole tired weight of him.

You put your arm round him. Your elbow's in the wrong place. You leave it there.

"You know how you change a bed with someone in it?" he says into your jacket. "You roll them. Like a carpet. He used to say *mind the merchandise*." A pause. "I got quite good."

A window full of nothing. A dead man watching. Every reason you gave for staying away is lined up behind your teeth, worn smooth. Work. The contract. The price of flights. And behind them, the real one.

*If you do not have TOLD,* you have never said it out loud to anyone. He hasn't asked. He might never ask. You could let this just be a hug.

*If you have TOLD,* he already knows it. He doesn't make you say it twice.

If you do not have the codeword TOLD, and you tell him now why you never came to the hospital, turn to {C16}.

If you say nothing, and just hold on until the frost has covered the glass, then walk him back up the Concourse, away from the white, turn to {C18}.
C16:
"It wasn't work," you say.

Sam doesn't move against you.

"It was never work. I told everyone it was work. I told you. I had the leave. I had the — I booked a flight. In March."

"March."

"I got as far as the gate, Sam." Your voice goes. It takes a while to come back. "I had the pass in my hand. And I turned round. And I went home."

"Why?"

"Because I—"

Nothing comes. You try again.

"I didn't want to see him. Like that. I wanted to keep him how he—" You can't finish it.

"So I let you. All of it. On your own." You can't look at him. "I knew. I knew I was doing it."

Sam steps out from under your arm.

For a second you think he's going to hit you. He opens his mouth and shuts it. Beyond the window, the white makes no sound at all.

"I was there," he says.

"I know."

"You don't. That's the point." His voice goes on the last word. "You know what I said, when he asked where you were? I told him you were busy. Every time. Busy."

You have nothing to give him back.

Sam grabs a fistful of your jacket at the chest and holds it, white-knuckled, the way you'd hold a rail on a train that's braking hard.

"I'm not done being angry," he says.

"I know."

He holds on. When at last he lets go, he turns his back on the window and walks, and you walk with him, back up the Concourse with the white behind you.

Lose 2 Fear. Note the codeword TOLD.

Turn to {C18}.
C14:
Sam makes a sound you've never heard from him, half sob and half a word. *Dad*, maybe. Or *wait*.

And he's moving. Towards the jet bridge door, the one he couldn't bring himself to touch a minute ago, both arms out for the push bar.

Beyond the glass, the man in the coat opens his arms.

Three years of not reaching for him. You reach now with everything you've got.

Test your Fortune. If you are Lucky, you catch the back of his jacket a whisker from the bar, and you haul him off his feet and away, and you don't stop pulling until Gates 00 is out of sight behind you; turn to {C18}. If you are Unlucky, turn to {C17}.
C17:
You grab for him and close on air.

Sam hits the push bar and the door swings open onto white, and he's through, and the door is closing behind him on its slow hydraulic arm, and you throw yourself at it.

It slams. The windows shiver and the frost leaps across the glass in a single sheet.

You pull the bar. Push it. Pull. It isn't locked. It isn't a door any more. It's a wall in the shape of one.

On the other side of the little window, the man in the coat is gone. So is Sam. There is only white.

*Ding-dong.*

Then Sam's voice, too close to the microphone, confused:

*Hello? Is this on? I can't see anything. It's really bright. Can you hear me? I can't—*

It cuts off with a click.

*Thank you,* says the Announcer warmly. *Sam.* A pause, and the scratch of a pen. *Checked in.*

Note the codeword LOST. You stand with your forehead on the cold steel until it goes numb. Because there's nothing else to do, you walk.

Turn to {C18}.
C18:
*If you have been here before,* one more coin in the fountain has turned face down since last time. Far behind you, the board in the Atrium clatters over. Choose below.

Otherwise: the Concourse opens into a round hall around a dry fountain, its basin carpeted with coins, every one face up. Off it lie a plain door marked *PRAYER ROOM*; the old smoking lounge, a glass box of yellow light and grey air; and a corridor towards Gate 9, where a child is crying.

If you haven't already been into the prayer room, and want to, turn to {C26}.

If you haven't already tried the smoking lounge, and want to, turn to {C29}.

If you haven't already followed the crying, and want to go towards Gate 9, turn to {C33}.

To leave the Concourse, tick one hour on your Adventure Sheet and go back up it to the Atrium: the clock there will have moved on without you.

If you have just ticked your sixth hour, turn to {E_FINALCALL}.

If you do not have the codeword RETURNED, turn to {H05}.

If you have RETURNED but not HEARD, turn to {H03}.

Otherwise turn to {H01}.
C26:
The door is heavy and closes behind you on a soft rush of air, and the airport goes away.

The prayer room is small and carpeted and lit low. No symbols, or all of them: a shelf of books in a dozen scripts, a rack of folded mats, a little table of tea lights in glass holders. One is already lit, apart from the others, its wax soft.

On the inside of the door, a sign lettered in careful capitals. *A PLACE FOR GOODBYES.*

For the first time all night, the airport's hum has gone. No board, no chime. Only your own heartbeat, slowing to match the room.

*If Sam is with you,* he picks up a tea light and the long lighter. He's shaking so much it takes four goes. He sets it down beside the one already burning. "For Dad," he says. "Sorry it's a rubbish one. They didn't have big ones." You laugh, and it hurts under your ribs.

Through the frosted panel in the door, a shape comes down the corridor. Tall. Too tall. It stops just beyond the glass, a dark blur of coat and a sign held up high, and stands there a long time.

It doesn't come in.

Lose 2 Fear.

When you look again, the shape has gone. Turn to {C18}.
C29:
The smoking lounge is a glass box against the Concourse wall, the kind they ripped out of airports years ago. Yellow light. Ashtrays on chrome poles. And smoke, so thick it presses against the glass.

It isn't drifting. It's standing. There are shapes in it, human height, human shoulders, a head turned this way, an arm lifting a cigarette to a mouth that isn't there. Some lean on the glass the way people lean when they're waiting for a flight. One of them waves to you.

On the ledge just inside the door lies a cigarette packet, soft and crushed at one corner. There's writing on it in biro. You can't read it through the haze.

You'd have to open the door. You'd have to reach in.

Dad had a rule for walking past the smokers outside the terminal. *Hold your breath, kids. Count to ten.*

*If Sam is with you,* he says it before you can, in Dad's voice, badly. "Hold your breath, kids."

You fill your lungs, open the door, and reach.

Test your Fortune. If you are Lucky, turn to {C27}.

If you are Unlucky, the smoke comes out to meet you. It pours into your face in one grey gust, tasting of stale ashtrays and airline coffee and other people's lungs, and you get the door shut on your knees, coughing, the packet gone. Lose 2 Vigour, and turn to {C18}.
C27:
You snatch the packet and you're out, the door sighing shut behind you, before the smoke has time to notice. A few grey threads curl after you across the carpet and come apart.

You smooth the packet out. The brand has been scratched off. Across the front, in hurried biro capitals:

*TRANSFERS: THE NUMBER YOU'RE ON IS THE WAY OFF.*

You read it twice. The number you're on. You turn it over in your head and can't see the other side yet.

Behind the glass, every shape in the smoke has turned to watch you. One of them taps two grey fingers against the pane, slowly, twice.

*If Sam is with you,* he leans in. "On what? I'm not on anything. I'm on four hours' sleep." He looks at the smoke, then back at the packet. "I hate this place. It talks in crossword clues."

Note the codeword TRANSFER. You put the packet away. Somewhere behind you, the child near Gate 9 is still crying. Turn to {C18}.
C33:
You follow the crying past Gate 9, and there she is.

A small child, four or five, sitting cross-legged on the carpet beneath a row of empty seats, in a yellow raincoat with the hood down. Her face is blotchy and wet. She's holding a cloth rabbit by one ear.

"I can't find my mum," she says, and hiccups. "She said wait here. She said she'd be one minute."

Every instinct you own says kneel. Ask her name. Find someone in a uniform. You can feel your knees wanting to bend.

The lights here are hard white strips, and every shadow under them is sharp and black. The seats cast shadows. The rabbit casts a little dangling one. Yours stretches long across the carpet.

The child casts none.

*If Sam is with you,* he has seen it too. He takes a step back and says your name, once, as a warning. *If you also have TRUCE,* he steps across instead, and puts himself between you and her.

"Please," she says, and holds up her arms to be lifted. "Please. I've been waiting so long."

If you kneel down to help her, turn to {C34}.

If you back away, slowly, turn to {C18}.
C34:
You kneel. You can't not. She's so small.

"Hey," you say. "It's all right. What's your mum's—"

She smiles at you. Then her face opens.

It opens from the hairline down, neatly, the way a zip opens, the two halves parting with a soft dry sound. There isn't a child inside. There are faces, grey and packed tight, and every one of them is looking at you, and every mouth is saying *mum*.

Small fingers close on your jacket. They are much stronger than a child's.

You tear free. You hear the fabric go. You're up and running, and behind you, unhurried, the crying starts again, the same as before, for the next one.

*If Sam is with you,* he's running in front of you, shouting at you to move, and he doesn't stop until the fountain.

Lose 3 Vigour. Gain 1 Fear.

Turn to {C18}.
